strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear real-world applications (recommendation systems, marketplaces, digital health)
Novel theoretical contributions: policy gradient analysis for nonstationary MDPs, explicit bias-variance bounds, and nonstationary CLT with consistent HAC variance estimator
Simple, practical estimator that requires only observed rewards without state observability, unlike existing OPE methods
Rigorous mathematical treatment with detailed proofs establishing bias bound O(k²δ²M + γ^k δM/(1-γ)) and variance bound
Comprehensive experimental validation across three levels of realism (two-state MDP, hospital queueing with real data, ride-sharing with real NYC taxi data)
Clear presentation with good use of figures (especially Figure 1) and comprehensive related work section
weaknesses: Truncation size k selection relies on heuristic Algorithm 1 rather than principled data-driven approach; optimal k varies with system parameters and is difficult to determine in practice
Practical parameter estimation is underspecified: How to estimate kernel deviation δ and mixing rate γ from data is not discussed; verification of Assumptions 1-3 is unclear
Finite state space assumption limits applicability; extension to continuous state spaces via discretization is not addressed
Mixed empirical results: In queueing case (Figure 4), bias-corrected (BC) estimator with tuned burn-in performs comparably to TPG; in ride-sharing (Figure 6), TPG's advantage over BC is modest
All experiments are simulated or semi-synthetic; lack of real A/B test results from actual platforms weakens claims of practical effectiveness
Mixing time assumption (Assumption 1) is strong, requiring geometric mixing; discussion of when it fails or how to verify it is limited
Policy gradient framework in Sections 4-5 adds considerable complexity without being essential for practitioners; the core idea of comparing k-step rewards is simple
Performance sensitivity to experimental design not fully explored: In Figure 6, DM's performance is highly sensitive to switchback interval choice, suggesting system design dominates method choice

strengths: Well-motivated problem: A/B testing in dynamic systems with temporal interference is practically important and understudied
Theoretically rigorous: Clear bias-variance decomposition (Theorem 1) with interpretable components (Taylor error vs. mixing bias), and CLT with practical variance estimator (Theorem 2)
Simple and practical: TPG estimator requires no state space knowledge, works with single trajectories, and can be applied post-experiment
Novel theoretical framework: Analysis of truncated policy gradients in nonstationary settings and connection to truncated Q-values (Proposition 3) is new
Comprehensive experimental setup: Incorporation of real-world data (patient arrivals, NYC taxi) into simulators demonstrates practical relevance
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The fundamental contribution is straightforward (compare k-step accumulated rewards instead of instantaneous outcomes), making this an incremental extension of existing policy gradient methods (Farias et al. 2022, Hu and Wager 2022)

Restrictive and unverifiable assumptions: Assumption 1 (uniform geometric mixing across all timesteps and distributions) is stronger than presented; finite state space requirement limits applicability to modern continuous-space systems; paper provides no diagnostic tests for verifying assumptions in practice

Non-monotone bias tradeoff lacks principled solution: Bias bound O(k²δ²M + γ^k/(1-γ)δM) requires balancing growing and decaying terms, but paper provides only ad-hoc heuristic (Algorithm 1) without theoretical justification or data-driven selection method

Weak experimental validation: All results are simulation-only with no real-world A/B test data; key results show marginal improvements (Figure 6: TPG and simpler DM estimator nearly equivalent at 1-hour interval with overlapping confidence intervals); BC estimator shown to be competitive despite claimed advantages

Insufficient practical guidance: Paper does not explain how to verify Assumption 1, choose k without ground truth, assess robustness when assumptions are violated, or determine when TPG is preferable to simpler alternatives

Incomplete comparisons and missing ablations: Limited comparison to recent OPE estimators, robust regression, bootstrap methods; no ablation studies; no analysis of TPG performance when Markovian assumption is violated

Restrictive additional assumptions: Assumptions 2-3 (variance existence and Cesàro-L² stability) introduce unexplained constraints; condition ∆²_T = o(T^{-1/3}) is non-intuitive and not validated empirically

strengths: Well-motivated problem at intersection of experimental design and dynamic systems; clearly articulates limitations of existing approaches with concrete examples

Strong theoretical contributions: elegant bias-variance decomposition (Theorem 1) with interpretable tradeoffs; novel nonstationary policy gradient analysis; rigorous CLT and nonstationary HAC variance estimator for single-trajectory data (Theorem 2)

Practical algorithm that is simple to implement (no state knowledge required, works with single trajectory, allows post-experiment analysis) with demonstrated applicability beyond Bernoulli A/B tests to switchback designs

Rigorous experimental validation across synthetic and real-world scenarios (2-state MDP, patient queueing with real data, NYC ride-sharing with real data); comprehensive baseline comparisons showing substantial empirical improvements
Technically sound proofs with careful handling of nonstationary dynamics, matrix perturbations, and mixing time properties; proper formalization of nonstationary concepts
Clear presentation with logical flow, effective use of figures (particularly Figure 1 connecting TPG to policy gradients and GATE), and appropriate positioning relative to prior work
weaknesses: Strong assumptions with limited robustness analysis: uniform mixing time assumption (Assumption 1) may not hold across all times and distributions; no empirical investigation of performance under assumption violations; finite state space assumption limits applicability to continuous domains

Truncation size selection is ad-hoc despite practical importance: Algorithm 1 requires choosing threshold α; non-monotone bias-variance tradeoff makes principled selection difficult; limited guidance for practitioners who don't know mixing rate γ a priori

Experimental evaluation has notable gaps: limited parameter exploration (treatment effect magnitude, horizon length T, initial distribution sensitivity); no computational cost analysis; insufficient robustness testing; only 1,000 trials in synthetic experiments without formal statistical tests

Finite-horizon setting and GATE definition: τ represents time-averaged treatment effect over [T] which doesn't converge under nonstationarity; limited guidance on how to choose T in practice or whether practitioners care about time-averaged versus time-specific effects

Assumptions 2-3 for CLT lack practical guidance: asymptotic variance existence and Cesàro-L² mean stability with o(T^{-1/3}) convergence are reasonable but opaque regarding when real systems satisfy these conditions

Theoretical contributions are somewhat incremental: applies standard policy gradient analysis and mixing time tools from prior work (Hu & Wager 2022, Farias et al. 2022) to new setting; nonstationary HAC estimator is technically solid but not groundbreaking

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing temporal interference and nonstationarity in A/B testing with clear real-world applications
Rigorous theoretical analysis with explicit bias-variance tradeoff characterization: reduces bias from O(T²δ²M) to O(k²δ²M) while introducing controlled mixing bias
Simple and practical method requiring only observed rewards without state observability or multiple independent trajectories
Novel theoretical contributions including policy gradient interpretation and nonstationary HAC variance estimator for single-trajectory data
Comprehensive empirical validation across three realistic scenarios (synthetic MDP, queueing with real hospital data, NYC taxi simulator)
Clear presentation with excellent intuitive figures (especially Figure 1) connecting TPG to policy gradients and the GATE
Establishes CLT for nonstationary environments, enabling valid statistical inference
weaknesses: Core idea of using k-step accumulated rewards is relatively intuitive; while theoretical analysis is solid, conceptual novelty is limited
Practical improvements over baselines are incremental: comparable to switchback BC in Case Study I, only more robust across interval choices in Case Study II
Limited guidance on selecting k, the critical hyperparameter: main text suggests vague heuristics, with rigorous approach relegated to appendix

Assumptions difficult to verify in practice: geometric mixing (Assumption 1) lacks practical verification guidance; technical regularity conditions (Assumptions 2-3) may not hold for highly nonstationary systems
Theoretical bounds contain unspecified constants in O(·) notation, limiting practical interpretation; no finite-sample complexity analysis or convergence rates
All experiments are simulations despite using real data components; no deployment results or field validation
Heavy notation (P^t_z, L^t_θ, Q^{t,k}_{1/2}) makes paper dense; state-independent value function representation could be introduced more carefully
Incomplete robustness analysis: no discussion of performance degradation when assumptions violated or sensitivity to misspecified k
Non-monotone relationship between bias and parameters δ, k deserves clearer discussion and guidance

strengths: Addresses a practically important and theoretically challenging problem: treatment effect estimation in dynamic, nonstationary systems with temporal interference
Provides comprehensive theoretical analysis including bias-variance bounds (Theorem 1), CLT (Theorem 2), and nonstationary HAC variance estimator with proofs that appear technically sound
Demonstrates computational simplicity and practical advantages: does not require state observability, operates on single trajectory data, and is straightforward to implement
Experiments span synthetic, queueing-based, and real NYC taxi data, demonstrating engagement with realistic nonstationary patterns
Policy gradient interpretation provides novel theoretical perspective linking truncation to policy optimization
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea of using k-step accumulated rewards rather than 1-step rewards is straightforward and natural. The policy gradient interpretation, while interesting, appears somewhat post-hoc and does not yield actionable new insights beyond the estimator itself

Critical unresolved problem of truncation size selection: (1) Bias bound is non-monotone in k, making a priori selection impossible; (2) Optimal k depends on unknown mixing rate γ (Figure 2); (3) Post-hoc heuristic (Algorithm 1) introduces another hyperparameter α requiring tuning (Table 3 shows sensitivity); (4) No practical method provided for estimating γ from data

Significant gap between theory and practice: Theory assumes k is fixed a priori. When k is selected from data (as necessary in practice), the data-dependent model selection is not theoretically analyzed. Marketing this as 'post-experiment analysis' is misleading since practitioners must still perform hyperparameter tuning

Weak and potentially unfair experimental comparisons: (1) DQ poor performance may reflect tuning/implementation rather than fundamental limitations with no details on hyperparameter selection; (2) Comparing TPG (Bernoulli design) to BC (switchback design) conflates design and estimator effects; (3) Ride-sharing results show interval length selection problem, not fundamental DM limitation; (4) Recent nonstationary methods (Wu et al. 2024b) underutilized despite being cited

Theoretical concerns: (1) Variance bound O((k+1)³M²/T) shows cubic growth in k, which is concerning but not adequately discussed; (2) Assumption 3 (Cesàro-L² stability) is opaque and its necessity unexplained; (3) Uniform mixing coefficient assumption is restrictive; (4) No sensitivity analysis for bandwidth LT = O(T¹/³) or robustness to assumption violations

Lack of practitioner guidance: Paper does not explain how to estimate γ, what to do if γ varies over time, when TPG is preferable to alternative experimental designs (e.g., switchback, which authors claim is difficult to implement but which are widely deployed), or how to handle multivariate treatments

Missing important comparisons: No adaptive methods for online k selection, limited engagement with recent nonstationary causal inference literature, no discussion of statistical efficiency loss from single trajectory vs. multiple trajectories in OPE

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing temporal interference and nonstationarity in A/B testing for dynamic systems
Elegant and simple TPG estimator that requires no state space knowledge and works from single trajectories
Strong theoretical contributions including explicit bias-variance decomposition (Theorem 1) and nonstationary CLT with HAC variance estimator (Theorem 2)
Insightful policy gradient interpretation connecting k-step aggregation to truncated policy gradients, providing principled guidance for estimator design
Comprehensive experimental validation on realistic systems with real data (patient arrivals, NYC taxi data) showing consistent improvements over multiple baselines
Attention to practical implementation details including post-hoc k-selection algorithm and variance estimation for confidence intervals
Clear presentation with effective use of figures to illustrate estimator relationships and thorough appendices with proofs and experimental details
weaknesses: Core technique (k-step reward aggregation) is straightforward; main novelty lies in interpretation and nonstationary analysis, which is somewhat incremental relative to k-step returns in RL

Restrictive assumptions: uniform mixing (Assumption 1) across all states/times, finite state space, and Cesàro-L² mean stability (Assumption 3) are difficult to verify in practice and limit applicability

Bias-variance tradeoff not fully resolved: no theoretically justified optimal k*; Algorithm 1 (Lepski-inspired) lacks theoretical guarantees in nonstationary settings and shifts hyperparameter problem to choice of α
Bounds presented in O(·) notation hide constants; when γ → 1 (slow mixing), bias term (1-γ^k)/(1-γ)² becomes very large for moderate k, limiting practical utility

Inadequate discussion of failure modes: no guidance on detecting problematic regimes (large δ, large γ) or when TPG dominates switchback designs; Case Study II shows BC switchback performs reasonably well

Experimental limitations: Case Study I uses simple birth-death chains; Case Study II has modest effect sizes; limited ablation studies on sensitivity to key parameters (M, δ, γ, T scaling); no comparison to neural network-based causal inference methods
Reproducibility concerns: claims code is 'publicly available' but no repository/link provided; k-selection algorithm remains somewhat ad-hoc despite heuristic approach
Scope limitations: focuses only on binary treatment, specific GATE definition; doesn't address heterogeneous treatment effects, spillover effects, or other treatment effect estimands
